key_claims: People who did around 90 to 120 minutes of strength training per week had about a 13% lower risk of dying from any cause compared to those who did none.
Strength training was linked to a 19% lower risk of dying from cardiovascular disease and a 27% lower risk of dying from neurological conditions.
Combining strength training with aerobic exercise was linked to about a 45% lower risk of death.
For cancer deaths, only smaller amounts of strength training (under an hour a week) were linked to lower risk.
The study was based on three long-running US studies following nearly 150,000 health professionals for up to 30 years.
limitations: The study was observational, so it cannot prove that strength training directly causes lower mortality.
Strength training was self-reported, and the study could not capture how hard people trained.
The study could not account for all potential confounding factors, though researchers adjusted for many including diet, smoking, and aerobic activity.
what_not_to_say: Strength training directly causes a longer life.
More than two hours of strength training per week provides additional benefits.
Strength training is more effective than aerobic exercise for reducing mortality.
The study proves that strength training reduces cancer mortality.
